title: What Logistics Teams in Morocco and the GCC Told Us in 2026: The 3 Transport Problems We Heard Most
summary: What logistics teams from more than 80 companies told us this year about planning, costs and systems, and why the same problems keep coming back.

It’s 6:30 in the morning. Orders came in overnight, two trucks are in maintenance, and a customer called to move a delivery. The planner opens the Excel file and starts again from yesterday’s plan. By 9:00, the trucks should have left.


This year, we heard versions of this morning in conversation after conversation.


**Three problems came back more than any others: plans built by hand, costs checked by hand, and systems that don’t cover transport. [→ Book a demo](https://freterium.ai/request-demo)**


### Who we spoke with


Over the past year, our team spoke with logistics and transport teams from more than 80 companies. They are shippers, distributors, retailers, manufacturers and logistics providers, in Morocco, the GCC and beyond. Some run their own fleet, some work only with carriers, most do both.


We asked the same question each time: what makes your transport day hard? The answers were surprisingly similar.


### Problem 1: the transport plan is built by hand


This was the problem we heard most. In many companies, the daily plan is built:


- **In Excel,** as orders come in, one line at a time
- **From memory,** by one experienced planner who knows “the routes”
- **Then sent by WhatsApp** or phone to drivers and carriers


Some teams told us it takes 2 to 3 hours every morning. When one truck is late or an urgent order arrives, the plan starts again.


The cost is not only the planner’s time. Trucks leave half full because nobody can compare options. And when the planner is away, the whole operation slows down.


### Problem 2: transport costs are checked by hand


Rate grids live in spreadsheets. Carrier invoices are checked line by line, often at the end of the month, weeks after the trips.


What we heard:


- One team found the same route priced at two different rates in its own grid.
- Another receives detention charges at least twice a week and checks each one by hand.
- Another spends 2 to 3 hours a month reconciling invoices from just three carriers.


When costs are checked this way, errors are found late, or not at all.


### Problem 3: the ERP doesn’t cover transport


Most companies we met already have an ERP such as SAP, Oracle or Sage. Some have a transport module, or an older TMS. Yet daily transport still runs next to it: in Excel, emails and phone calls.


As one prospect put it, as soon as something isn’t covered, “people go straight to Excel”. The data that would show what transport really costs is scattered across files and messages.


### Also on the list


Other problems came up often enough to note:


- **Ageing trucks and maintenance followed on paper.** One company told us its trucks older than 10 years are about 30% of the fleet but about 60% of breakdowns.
- **No real-time view of trucks,** even when they have GPS. One shipper estimated that only about 70% of its carriers’ GPS data was usable.
- **Proof of delivery that comes back days later.** One distributor needed 5 to 6 days to confirm that an order was delivered.
- **Trucks leaving half full** and returning empty.
- **Wrong or missing customer addresses,** which break routes and tracking.


### Why these problems last


None of these teams lacked skill. Their planners know their customers, their roads and their carriers better than any software. The problems last for simpler reasons:


- **The work happens every day,** so there is never time to step back and change it.
- **Excel and WhatsApp are free and flexible,** and they work, until volumes grow.
- **Transport sits between systems:** the ERP handles orders and payments, the carriers handle trucks, and the daily coordination falls in between.


### Key takeaways


- The most common transport problem we heard is the daily plan built by hand.
- Transport costs and carrier invoices are often checked by hand, weeks after the trips.
- Having an ERP doesn’t mean transport is covered: daily coordination often runs in Excel and messages.
- These problems last because they are daily, cheap to keep, and sit between systems.

### FAQ


**Which transport problems do logistics teams in Morocco and the GCC face most?**
In our conversations with more than 80 companies, the three most frequent were plans built by hand in Excel, transport costs checked by hand, and ERPs that don’t cover daily transport operations.


**Why do companies with an ERP still plan transport in Excel?**
ERPs manage orders, stock and finance well, but daily planning, carrier coordination and delivery tracking often fall outside them.


**How much time do teams spend on manual transport planning?**
Several teams we spoke with told us 2 to 3 hours every morning, before any problem on the road.


**Why is proof of delivery still on paper in many companies?**
Because drivers and carriers often have no shared tool. The paper note has to travel back to the office before anyone can confirm the delivery.


**Do these problems affect companies with their own fleet or with carriers?**
Both. Companies with their own fleet mention maintenance and planning more; those using carriers mention costs, invoices and visibility more.
